Mount Erebus. Located on Ross Island in Antarctica, Mount Erebus is the southernmost active volcano on Earth and the second-highest volcano in Antarctica. It was discovered in 1841 by British explorer Sir James Clark Ross, who named the volcano and its nearby extinct neighbor, Mount Terror, after his expedition's two ships, HMS Erebus and HMS Terror. The volcano is famous for its persistent, convective lava lake of rare phonolitic lava, one of only a handful of long-lived lava lakes active on Earth today. Mount Erebus features unique ice towers, or fumaroles, on its upper slopes. These are hollow ice chimneys created when warm, sulfurous geothermal steam rises through vents and freezes in the sub-zero Antarctic air. The volcano's summit was the site of the tragic Air New Zealand Flight 901 disaster on November 28, 1979. A sightseeing flight crashed into the mountain's lower slope due to a coordinates error and sector whiteout, killing all 257 passengers and crew. Mount Erebus shares high-altitude characteristics with Mount Cotopaxi, another high-altitude active volcano notable for its glaciers and ice features, and resembles Mauna Loa, a massive shield volcano located in the Pacific.
